k-properties-s1.title: Two reactions of nitrogen oxides
k-properties-s1.text: A student is given Kc values for two reactions at 25 °C and wants Kc for related reactions at 25 °C.

k-properties-s2.title: K at different temperatures
k-properties-s2.text: Kc for N2O4(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g) is measured at four temperatures.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: reversing a reaction does not change the sign of K. Take the reciprocal: 1/K.
Value: you took a square root. The coefficients are unchanged; only the direction is reversed, so use 1/K.

why.correct: This is reaction B reversed, so K = 1/K<sub>B</sub> = 1 / (6.0 × 10¹³) = 1.7 × 10<sup>−14</sup>.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for NO(g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ NO<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: halving the coefficients does not halve K. It raises K to the power ½: take the square root.
Value: you squared K. Halving the coefficients takes the square root.

why.correct: Reaction B with every coefficient halved: K = (K<sub>B</sub>)<sup>1/2</sup> = √(6.0 × 10¹³) = 7.7 × 10<sup>6</sup>.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you added the K values. When reactions are added, their K values are multiplied.
Value: you divided. Adding reaction A to reaction B means multiplying K<sub>A</sub> by K<sub>B</sub>.

why.correct: Add reaction A to reaction B: 2 NO cancels, leaving N₂ + 2 O₂ ⇌ 2 NO₂. K = K<sub>A</sub> × K<sub>B</sub> = (4.5 × 10⁻³¹)(6.0 × 10¹³) = 2.7 × 10<sup>−17</sup>.

items.q: Which operation gives K<sub>c</sub> for 4 NO(g) ⇌ 2 N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: (1/K<sub>A</sub>)<sup>2</sup>
2/(K<sub>A</sub>)
(K<sub>A</sub>)<sup>2</sup>
−2K<sub>A</sub>

why.correct: Reversing gives the reciprocal; multiplying all coefficients by n raises K to the n. Together: (1/K<sub>A</sub>)².
options: Right: reverse reaction A (1/K<sub>A</sub>), then double every coefficient (square it).
Doubling the equation squares K; it does not multiply K by 2.
This doubles reaction A but does not reverse it. The new reaction has NO as the reactant.
Neither reversing nor doubling makes K negative or multiplies it by 2.

items.q: Using the values in the table, is N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) product-favored at this temperature?
options: No: K = 2.7 × 10<sup>−17</sup>, far below 1.
Yes: reaction B has a large K, so the overall reaction does too.
Yes: K = 6.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> + 4.5 × 10<sup>−31</sup>, which is large.
It is undecided, because K<sub>A</sub> and K<sub>B</sub> point in opposite directions.

why.correct: K(overall) = K<sub>A</sub>K<sub>B</sub> = 2.7 × 10<sup>−17</sup> ≪ 1, so the overall reaction is reactant-favored.
options: Right: the tiny K of reaction A outweighs the large K of reaction B when they are multiplied.
The overall K is the product of both K values. 10⁻³¹ × 10¹³ is still very small.
K values of added reactions are multiplied, not added.
It can: multiply them. The result is far below 1.

items.q: A flask at 350 K holds an equilibrium mixture. More N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is injected and the flask is held at 350 K. What is K<sub>c</sub> once equilibrium is restored?
options: Greater than 0.13, because more N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> reacts.
Less than 0.13, because there is more reactant on the bottom of the expression.
1.5, because the system shifts to the next K in the table.

why.correct: At a fixed temperature, K is a constant. Adding N₂O₄ lowers Q below K, and the net forward reaction restores Q = K = 0.13.
options: Right: K depends only on temperature. Adding a reactant changes Q and the concentrations, not K.
More N₂O₄ reacts, but the new concentrations still satisfy the same K. K itself does not move.
Right after the injection, Q is below 0.13. The system then reacts forward until Q is back at 0.13.
K changes only if the temperature changes. Here it stays at 350 K.

items.q: What does the table show about this reaction as the temperature rises?
options: It becomes more product-favored.
It becomes more reactant-favored.
It reaches equilibrium more slowly.
Its K stays the same, but its Q increases.

why.correct: A larger K means more product at equilibrium. Here K rises with temperature, so the equilibrium mixture holds more NO₂ at higher temperatures.
options: Right: K grows from 7.1 × 10⁻³ to 10. as the temperature goes from 298 K to 450 K.
K is rising, which means more NO₂ relative to N₂O₄ at equilibrium.
The table gives K, which says nothing about speed.
K is clearly changing in the table. Q depends on the mixture, not on the temperature alone.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) at 400 K.

mistakes.why: Value: this is K for the forward direction. Reversing a reaction gives 1/K.
Value: reversing does not make K negative. Take the reciprocal.

items.q: A student says K<sub>c</sub> increased from 298 K to 450 K because more N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> was added in the hotter trials. Which response is best?
options: Wrong: K changed because the temperature changed.
Right: K grows when there is more reactant to react.
Right: at higher temperatures there are more molecules, so K rises.
Wrong: K is a fixed number, so the table contains an error.

why.correct: For a given reaction, K changes only with temperature. Changing amounts changes Q, and the system shifts to restore the same K.
options: Right: K depends on temperature alone for a given reaction. Concentrations shift to fit K, never the other way.
More reactant changes Q, and the system then re-establishes the same K.
Heating a sealed flask does not add molecules. The K values differ because the temperatures differ.
K does change, but only when the temperature does. The table is fine.

items.q: For 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = K. What is K<sub>c</sub> for SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ SO<sub>3</sub>(g)?
options: K<sup>1/2</sup>
2K

why.correct: Multiplying an equation by n raises K to the n. Here n = ½, so K becomes √K.
options: Right: halving every coefficient raises K to the power ½.
Coefficients are exponents in K, so halving them takes a square root, not half.
This would follow from treating coefficients as multipliers, which they are not.
That is the reversed reaction, not the halved one.

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 50.0 at 450 °C. Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for HI(g) ⇌ ½ H<sub>2</sub>(g) + ½ I<sub>2</sub>(g) at 450 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: reversing gives 1/50.0, but you also halved the equation. Take the square root as well.
Value: halving an equation takes a square root; it does not divide K by 2.
Value: you halved the equation but did not reverse it. Take the reciprocal too.

items.q: Given: (1) A(g) ⇌ B(g), K<sub>1</sub> = 1.4 × 10<sup>−2</sup>; (2) B(g) ⇌ 2 C(g), K<sub>2</sub> = 6.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Calculate K for A(g) ⇌ 2 C(g).

mistakes.why: Value: when reactions add, their K values multiply.
Value: neither reaction is reversed, so multiply the K values rather than dividing.

why.correct: Adding (1) and (2) cancels B: A ⇌ 2 C. K = K₁K₂ = (1.4 × 10⁻²)(6.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 8.4 × 10<sup>−7</sup>.

items.q: Given: CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>1</sub>; and CH<sub>4</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>2</sub>. Which gives K for CH<sub>4</sub>(g) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 4 H<sub>2</sub>(g)?
options: K<sub>1</sub>K<sub>2</sub>
K<sub>1</sub> + K<sub>2</sub>
K<sub>2</sub> / K<sub>1</sub>
(K<sub>1</sub> × K<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>

why.correct: Adding the two equations as written cancels CO and combines the H₂O (1 + 1 = 2) and H₂ (3 + 1 = 4), giving the target exactly. Equations added, K values multiplied.
options: Right: the two equations add directly (CO cancels) to give the target, so multiply.
Adding equations multiplies K values; adding K values matches the ΔH rule for Hess’s law, not K.
Dividing would mean one reaction was reversed. Here both are used as written.
No coefficients were doubled, so no exponent is needed.

items.q: Hess’s law (topic 6.9) says ΔH values add when equations add. Why are K values multiplied instead?
options: K is a product of terms, so shared terms cancel.
K values are larger in size than ΔH values are.
K depends on temperature and ΔH does not.
Multiplying is used so the units of K cancel.

why.correct: K is products over reactants, a product of terms. Writing K₁ × K₂ cancels any species that appears on top of one and bottom of the other, leaving exactly the expression for the summed reaction.
options: Right: multiplying the two expressions cancels the shared species and gives the expression for the overall reaction.
Size has nothing to do with it. The rule comes from how K is built.
Both depend on temperature to some extent; that is not why the rules differ.
K has no units on the exam. The rule comes from the form of the expression.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 0.50 at a certain temperature. Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 6 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 4 NH<sub>3</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: doubling the equation squares K; it does not double it.

items.q: Which changes alter the value of K<sub>c</sub> for a given reaction equation? Select all that apply.
options: Changing the temperature
Adding more of a reactant
Changing the volume of the container
Adding a catalyst

why.correct: For a given equation, K changes only with temperature. Writing the equation differently (reversed, scaled) gives a different K, but that is a different equation.
options: Right: K depends on temperature.
This changes Q and the concentrations, not K.
Volume changes concentrations (and Q), not K.
A catalyst speeds both directions equally and leaves K unchanged.
